Sophie works in a busy policy team in the civil service. She’s in charge of ordering food for an upcoming cross-departmental meeting. Normally, when the team gets external sandwiches delivered, the standard lunch option costs £12 per person.

A few days before the meeting, Sophie gets an email from the finance officer reminding everyone of a small budget squeeze this quarter. It isn’t drastic, but they’re asked to trim non-essential spending where possible.

Sophie looks at the catering menu again and notices that the same supplier offers a “lighter lunch” option, smaller sandwiches and fewer extras for £8 per person. It’s a £4 reduction from what she had planned, and still perfectly suitable for a two-hour meeting.

She switches to the cheaper option, sends the revised cost to finance, and gets a quick “thanks for being mindful of the budget” reply. On the day of the meeting, people barely notice the change, everyone eats, the meeting runs smoothly, and the team stays within budget without any fuss.
column29:
Aaron works in a strategy unit in the civil service and is organising the monthly stakeholder roundtable. He always orders the same catering package: a standard lunch selection that costs £12 per person. It’s reliable, everyone likes it, and it fits neatly within the team’s recurring events budget.

This month, Aaron briefly considers switching things up, maybe a lighter option or something fancier, but after checking the attendance list and the budget, he realises nothing has changed. The meeting is the usual length, the participants are the same mix of internal and external attendees, and the budget is exactly what it has always been.

So he decides to keep the order exactly as it is, making no change to the £12-per-person cost. The team knows what to expect, the catering arrives as usual, and everything runs smoothly. It’s a routine choice, just sticking with what already works.
column30:
Tom, a civil servant in his mid thirties, is coordinating a workshop with colleagues from several departments. He usually does a quick coffee run beforehand to keep everyone energised. The cafe near the office charges £12 for a box of mixed pastries to go with the drinks.

This month, Tom’s team has been reminded to be extra careful with small discretionary expenses. Looking at the receipts from previous workshops, Tom realises the pastries are nice, but not essential, especially because people often only take one or skip them entirely.

When he checks the café’s menu again, he notices they sell a simple biscuit selection for £4. It’s not as exciting, but it’s still something to have with coffee. Choosing it instead of the pastries saves £8, which fits perfectly with the 'spend wisely' message.

On the day, his colleagues shrug and laugh: Biscuit day today, is it? The workshop goes well, everyone gets what they need, and Tom feels good knowing he made a sensible cut without hurting the atmosphere.

Maria is a single mum with two kids, ages 6 and 9. After a long day juggling work and school pickups, she decides to treat them to a quick takeaway dinner. Their usual go to is a £12 family meal from the local chicken place, nothing fancy, but it feeds all three of them.

But this week, money is a bit tighter. The car needed an unexpected repair, and she’s trying to make her budget stretch until payday. When she opens the delivery app, she notices the same restaurant offers a smaller family deal for £6 less, at £6. It has fewer sides and smaller portions, but still enough for the kids, and she knows she can make something simple for herself at home.

She chooses the cheaper option, saving £6. The kids still get their favourite chicken and chips, and Maria feels a small wave of relief, she managed to treat them while staying sensible with her money.

Later, as they sit around the table laughing about the day, she’s reminded that even with a tighter budget, she can still create little moments of comfort for her family.
